items.prompt: What does 'expected value' compute?
choices: For each possible outcome, probability times payoff/cost, summed across all outcomes
The single most likely outcome
The worst possible outcome across all options
The average of the raw cost numbers, ignoring probability
items.explanation: Expected value weights each outcome by how likely it is before summing -- it isn't the most likely single outcome, the worst case, or a plain average that ignores probability.
items.reference:
Σ EV = sum of (probability × payoff) across every outcome
🎯 not the most likely outcome, not the worst case

Why: EV is a weighted average across the whole outcome set, not a pick of any single outcome.

items.prompt: Which of these correctly describes how to compute expected value for a decision with several possible outcomes?
choices: Multiply each outcome's probability by its payoff/cost, then add all those products together
Add up all the probabilities and multiply by the highest possible cost
Take the median of all possible costs
Ignore probabilities and just average the costs
items.explanation: EV is the sum of (probability x payoff) across outcomes -- not a median of costs, not probabilities multiplied by only the highest cost, and not a plain unweighted average.
items.reference:
Σ EV = sum of (probability × payoff) across every outcome
🎯 not the most likely outcome, not the worst case

Why: EV is a weighted average across the whole outcome set, not a pick of any single outcome.

items.prompt: What is a 'tail outcome'?

items.explanation: A tail outcome sits at the extreme end of a distribution -- unlikely, but with impact large enough to matter disproportionately, like the 20%-chance, $60,000 outage.

items.prompt: Why does EV work well for a casino running the same game millions of times?
choices: With enough repetitions, the law of large numbers means actual results converge tightly around the expected value
Because casinos always have a 100% chance of winning
Because casino games have no variance
Each individual hand is guaranteed to hit exactly the expected value
items.explanation: Any single hand has real variance, but across millions of hands, the law of large numbers smooths that variance out so revenue converges around EV -- EV is the right frame precisely because of the repetition, not because any one hand is risk-free.
items.reference:
🎰 casino / insurer: many repetitions → EV is the right frame
🚀 one-shot startup bet: no repetitions → EV alone is dangerous

Why: EV describes what happens on average over many repetitions -- a decision-maker who only gets one repetition never actually gets that average.
